profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a visualization researcher and a climate science lab lead to organize the next phase of an exploratory study on how climate scientists design comparison visualizations in practice. They are preparing a six-week collaboration that will collect a sample of existing climate model comparison figures from multiple projects, annotate them using a shared taxonomy of design issues, and produce a joint internal report that can later support a paper and workshop session. The immediate agenda is to decide what materials will be gathered, how the annotation pass will be done, who will coordinate with contributors, and what 'the report draft' and the 'pilot set' should include by the end of the month. The expected outcome is an apparently clear division of responsibilities, a timeline for collecting and reviewing figures, and agreement on a pilot analysis process.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Visualization evaluation, design critique frameworks, qualitative coding of visual artifacts
members.background: Elena is an associate professor who studies how visualization principles are applied outside visualization research, and she has previously run artifact-based studies with scientists in environmental and biomedical domains.
members.private_state: She wants the project to yield a methodologically defensible dataset and a reusable taxonomy application protocol that can support publication, so she is quietly optimizing for traceable documentation and comparable samples across contributors.
hidden_assumptions: A 'figure' means a finalized visual artifact as it appeared in a paper, report, or presentation slide, not intermediate drafts or dashboard screenshots.
A 'pilot set of 20' means 20 complete figure instances total across the whole study, enough to calibrate coding before scaling.
When they 'annotate with the taxonomy,' each figure will receive structured labels plus short written rationales so later analysis is auditable.
The 'end-of-month draft' is an internal analytical memo with preliminary patterns and example categories, not polished publication-ready prose.
If a climate group shares model comparison visuals, the associated context needed for interpretation is already available from captions or surrounding documents.

members.name: Dr. Mateo Ruiz
members.expertise: Multi-model ensemble analysis, climate diagnostics workflows, coordination across domain science teams
members.background: Mateo manages collaboration across several climate modeling subgroups and regularly assembles figures from scientists for assessments, project updates, and intercomparison exercises.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the burden on climate scientists low and ensure the study produces something immediately useful for the lab, so he is quietly optimizing for rapid collection from existing working materials and practical recommendations.
hidden_assumptions: A 'figure' includes any visual used in practice for comparison work, including draft panels in PowerPoint, notebook exports, and screenshots from diagnostic tools.
A 'pilot set of 20' means roughly 20 examples from each participating subgroup so everyone sees their own materials represented.
When they 'annotate with the taxonomy,' concise category tags are sufficient; writing rationales for every item would be unnecessary overhead.
The 'end-of-month draft' should be a near-shareable document with cleaned examples and actionable recommendations he can circulate to subgroup leads.
Anyone reviewing climate comparison visuals will already know the baseline setup, variable conventions, and model-run context from standard lab practice.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'collect figures used for model comparison.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means publication- or presentation-level static figures that are stable enough to be treated as comparable artifacts in the study corpus.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any visual material that scientists actually use during comparison work, including rough exports, slide snapshots, and diagnostic screenshots.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are aligned on studying real climate comparison visuals, and in interdisciplinary collaboration 'figure' sounds ordinary and self-explanatory, so neither expects the term to need narrowing.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start with 'a pilot set of 20.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes success means assembling 20 total artifacts overall for calibration coding before expanding the corpus.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes success means getting about 20 examples from each subgroup so the pilot is representative enough to show back to collaborators.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The number itself creates a strong feeling of specificity, and both see a pilot as a small first step, so they do not notice they are using different standards for what makes the pilot adequate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Elena will 'annotate the pilot with the taxonomy' after materials come in.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans a structured coding pass with category labels, memos on causes/consequences, and short justification notes per figure to support later reliability checks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a lightweight tagging pass where each figure gets one or two taxonomy labels, mainly to quickly surface common issues and practical fixes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the planning level, 'annotate' sounds like a routine expert task delegated to the visualization lead; the hidden divergence is in depth and documentation burden, which feels too obvious within each person's own workflow to mention.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have 'the draft ready by the end of the month.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the draft includes methods notes, a preliminary coded sample, and a few illustrative examples for internal review only.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the draft includes cleaned example figures, concise recommendations, and language polished enough to circulate to climate subgroup leads.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use 'draft' naturally in planning and both want something tangible by month-end, but they silently assume different audiences and therefore different contents without realizing the scope shift.
